Q: ImportError: cannot import name 'create_tool_calling_agent' from 'langchain.agents' A:

your referenced example is from a older verison of langchain and perhaps, you're using the new version. That's why you get the ImportError.

create_tool_calling_agent was removed in LangChain v0.2+ and is not available in langchain.agents in recent version.

You can use create_agent from langchain.agents instead, which is the new standard for building tool-calling agents in LangChain v1. It runs on LangGraph under the hood and supports the ReAct loop for tool calling.

for example:

from langchain.agents import create_agent
from langchain_core.tools import tool  # or your tools

# Example tool
@tool
def example_tool(query: str) -> str:
    """Example tool."""
    return f"Result for {query}"

# Create agent (replace 'gpt-4o-mini' with your model string or ChatModel instance)
agent = create_agent(
    model="gpt-4o-mini",  # or ChatOpenAI(model="gpt-4o-mini")
    tools=[example_tool],
    system_prompt="You are a helpful assistant with access to tools."  # Optional
)

# Invoke
result = agent.invoke({"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Use the tool!"}]})

Key differences from the old API(create_tool_calling_agent):

  • No separate prompt - use system_prompt (string or SystemMessage)
  • Input is {"messages": [...]} dict
  • Built-in streaming, persistence, structured output via response_format
  • Add middleware for advanced features (dynamic prompts, moderation, etc.)

But, if you want to use create_tool_calling_agent, you can try langchain-classic

This package was created to provide backward compatibility for existing applications that were not yet ready to migrate to the new v1.0 APIs.

references:

  • https://reference.langchain.com/python/langchain_classic/agents/
  • ImportError: cannot import name 'AgentExecutor' from 'langchain.agents'

Q: C# MySQL SSL Connection Error when trying to use conn.Open() A:

In case anyone is wondering why the accepted answer doesn't work for recent MySQL installations:

ssl mode=none was deprecated here: https://dev.mysql.com/doc/relnotes/connector-net/en/news-8-0-29.html and renamed to ssl mode=disabled.

Q: Is it necessary your Python function should have return in? A:

Let's take your questions at face value:

Is it necessary your Python function should have return in?

No, that's not necessary. If you omit the return statement, it will implicitly return None. This has been answered in python: return, return None, and no return at all -- is there any difference?

Should I add another return inside the function or is this correct?

Last question first: yes, this is correct.

Which leaves us with:

Should I add another return inside the function[?]

Imagine code like this (and don't do it!):

def odd_or_even(n):
    if n % 2 != 0:
        return "Odd"
    else:
        return "Even"
    return "Now what here?"

This line can never be reached. As commented, this adds one unnecessary line to your function (or: every function if you make this a general principle) which can never be reached, does nothing and only serves to puzzle future readers of your code. It's not wrong, it's just ill-advised.

Let's imagine the trailing return could be reached. What should it return? We now know n is neither odd nor even, what is it? We don't even know what to return at this point. If anything, you could assert or raise an exception to signal your program ran into an "impossible" state. This may happen if your control flow consists of several conditions and you expect exactly one of them to return.

From a practical point of view, omitting the else and de-indenting the return as answered by adshin21 is the way to go. This gives you an unconditional return on the last line. It will also satisfy pylint which would otherwise complain that ...

R1705 (no-else-return) Unnecessary "else" after "return", remove the "else" and de-indent the code inside it

If we take pylint's warnings as a guide to idiomatic code, this is the way to go.

To communicate that you want to unconditionally want to return from the function, it's even more clear to use a ternary as commented by Konrad Rudolph
